concepts.name: Sound
concepts.statement: Sound is a disturbance of matter that is transmitted from its source outward, and it is a wave. On the atomic scale it is a disturbance of atoms that is far more ordered than their thermal motions, and in many instances it is a periodic wave in which the atoms undergo simple harmonic motion.

concepts.name: Sound as a pressure wave
concepts.statement: A vibrating string compresses the air in front of it and expands the air behind it, and these compressions and rarefactions move out as longitudinal pressure waves with the frequency of the string. Sound waves in air and most fluids are longitudinal because fluids have almost no shear strength. A graph of gauge pressure against distance from the source is a sine wave, and for ordinary sounds the pressure varies only slightly from atmospheric. The amplitude decreases with distance for three reasons. The energy spreads over a larger area, objects such as the eardrum absorb it, and the viscosity of air and heat transfer between compressions and rarefactions turn it into thermal motion.

concepts.name: Hearing
concepts.statement: Hearing is the perception of sound, just as vision is the perception of visible light. The physical phenomenon and its perception are related but not the same thing, and the chapter keeps them apart: wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed of propagation belong to the wave, and pitch and loudness belong to the listener.

concepts.name: Pitch
concepts.statement: Perception of frequency is called pitch. You sense the frequency of a sound directly, and the wavelength only indirectly, through the size of a musical instrument. Small instruments such as a piccolo make high-pitch, short-wavelength sounds, and large instruments such as a tuba make low-pitch, long-wavelength ones.

concepts.name: Speed of sound, frequency and wavelength
concepts.statement: The relationship of the speed of sound, its frequency and its wavelength is the same as for all waves. The wavelength is the distance between adjacent identical parts of the wave, for example between adjacent compressions, and the frequency is that of the source, the number of waves that pass a point per unit time. In a given medium under fixed conditions the speed is constant, so the higher the frequency, the smaller the wavelength.

concepts.name: Speed of sound in different media
concepts.statement: The speed of sound in a medium is determined by a combination of the medium's rigidity, or compressibility in gases, and its density. The more rigid or less compressible the medium, the faster the speed of sound, and for materials of similar rigidity sound travels faster through the one with the lower density. The speed of sound in air is low because air is compressible, and it is generally greater in liquids and solids. Earthquakes show the same dependence: longitudinal P-waves outrun transverse S-waves in granite because its bulk modulus is greater than its shear modulus.

concepts.name: Speed of sound and temperature
concepts.statement: For air at sea level the speed of sound is 331 m/s at 0 °C and grows as the square root of the kelvin temperature. The speed of sound in a gas follows the average speed of its particles, which itself goes as the square root of the temperature. The dependence is real but not strong: at 20.0 °C the speed is 343 m/s, less than a 4% increase.

forms.condition: air at sea level, T in kelvin

concepts.name: Speed of sound and frequency
concepts.statement: In open air the speed of sound is the same for all frequencies in the audible range. If it were not, the music of a marching band would arrive out of cadence, the low-pitch instruments lagging the high-pitch ones more the farther away you stood; because all instruments arrive together at any distance, all frequencies travel at nearly the same speed, and so a fixed speed ties frequency and wavelength together.

concepts.name: Frequency across media
concepts.statement: When sound travels from one medium to another its speed changes, but its frequency usually remains the same, because it is like a driven oscillation and has the frequency of the original source. Since the speed changes and the frequency does not, the wavelength must change: the higher the speed of sound, the greater the wavelength for a given frequency.

concepts.name: Finding a distance from an echo
concepts.statement: A bat uses sound echoes to find its way about and to catch prey, and sonar and medical imaging use them the same way. The sound travels out and back at the speed of sound in the medium, so the time for an echo to return is directly proportional to the distance. The precision of the echo time sets the smallest difference in distance you can resolve.

concepts.name: Sound intensity
concepts.statement: Intensity is the power per unit area carried by a wave, where power is the rate at which the wave transfers energy, and its SI unit is the watt per metre squared. It is the physical quantity behind loudness, and it applies to every sound, audible or not. The intensities of ordinary sounds are small: only about 10⁻¹⁶ W falls on the eardrum at the threshold of hearing.

concepts.name: Intensity and pressure amplitude
concepts.statement: The intensity of a sound wave is proportional to its amplitude squared. The pressure amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum pressure in the wave, the density is that of the material the sound travels in, and the speed is the speed of sound in that medium. The energy of an oscillating element of air is proportional to its amplitude squared, and the pressure variation is proportional to the amplitude of the oscillation. The intensity therefore goes as the square of the pressure amplitude: the greater the amplitude, the more the sound compresses the air.

concepts.name: Sound intensity level
concepts.statement: We quote sound intensity levels in decibels much more often than intensities in watts per metre squared, because the logarithm of the intensity describes how our ears perceive sound better than the intensity itself. The level of a sound of intensity $I$ is ten times the logarithm of its ratio to the reference intensity $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m². Because it is a ratio, the level is unitless and gives the sound relative to a fixed standard. The "deci" in decibel says that the ratio's logarithm is multiplied by ten.

concepts.name: Threshold of hearing
concepts.statement: The reference intensity $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m² is the lowest intensity of sound a person with normal hearing can perceive at a frequency of 1000 Hz, and its level is 0 dB because the logarithm of one is zero. The ear is sensitive to as little as a trillionth of a watt per metre squared, when the air molecules vibrate over less than one molecular diameter and the gauge pressures are less than 10⁻⁹ atm, and it tolerates sounds 10¹² times as intense; a range that wide is why the logarithmic scale fits experience better than the intensities themselves.

concepts.name: Intensity ratios in decibels
concepts.statement: Each factor of 10 in intensity corresponds to 10 dB, so a 90 dB sound is three factors of 10, or 1000 times, as intense as a 60 dB sound. Because the logarithm of a ratio is the difference of the logarithms, the difference in level between two sounds depends only on the ratio of their intensities: doubling the intensity raises the level by about 3 dB and a factor of five raises it by 7 dB, whatever the intensities themselves are.

concepts.name: Adding the intensities of sources
concepts.statement: When many sources sound together and interference can be neglected, their intensities add, and the level rises by ten times the logarithm of how many there are: a thousand flies at 40.0 dB each make 70.0 dB, and ten stereos making 120 dB at the centre of a circle each contribute 110 dB. The rule is the decibel relation applied to a ratio that is a count.

concepts.name: Sound pressure level
concepts.statement: Another decibel scale, the sound pressure level, uses the ratio of the pressure amplitude to a reference pressure rather than of intensity to a reference intensity. It is common where sound travels in water, and it can give very different decibel numbers for the same sound. Ocean noise from ships may be 200 dB as a sound pressure level where the sound intensity level would be under 140 dB. Its numbers run 60 to 70 dB above the levels this text uses, as 17.7 notes.

concepts.name: Doppler effect
concepts.statement: The Doppler effect is an alteration in the observed frequency of a sound due to motion of either the source or the observer, and the actual change in frequency is the Doppler shift. Each compression spreads out spherically from the point where the source emitted it. When the source moves, the point of emission moves, so the compressions are closer together ahead of the source and farther apart behind it. The medium fixes the speed of sound, so a shorter wavelength arrives as a higher frequency. When the observer moves instead, the rate at which she meets the compressions changes. Relative motion toward one another raises the received frequency, motion apart lowers it, and the greater the relative speed, the greater the effect.

concepts.name: Doppler shift for a moving source
concepts.statement: For a stationary observer and a moving source, the frequency received is the source frequency times the ratio of the speed of sound to the speed of sound plus or minus the source's speed along the line joining them, the minus sign for motion toward the observer and the plus sign for motion away. The greater the speed of the source, the greater the effect, and the shifts toward and away are not symmetric.

forms.condition: stationary observer, moving source; minus for motion toward the observer, plus for motion away

concepts.name: Doppler shift for a moving observer
concepts.statement: For a stationary source and a moving observer, the received frequency is the source frequency times the ratio of the speed of sound plus or minus the observer's speed to the speed of sound. The plus sign is for motion toward the source and the minus sign for motion away. The form differs from the moving-source case because the observer passes through more or fewer crests of a wave whose wavelength stays the same.

forms.condition: stationary source, moving observer; plus for motion toward the source, minus for motion away

concepts.name: Doppler shift for source and observer moving
concepts.statement: When both move relative to the air there are two Doppler shifts, one for the moving observer and one for the moving source, and the received frequency is the product of the two factors. Source and observer carried together, as an engineer and the horn of the same train, receive the emitted frequency unchanged because the factors cancel; what matters is that they are not moving relative to each other.

concepts.name: Sonic booms
concepts.statement: As a source's speed approaches the speed of sound, the observed frequency ahead of it approaches infinity, because each successive wave piles onto the previous one. If the source exceeds the speed of sound, no sound reaches an observer until the source has passed. The waves interfere constructively along the lines of a cone, and this superposition is a sonic boom, a constructive interference of sound created by an object moving faster than sound. Inside the cone the interference is mostly destructive. The faster the source, the smaller the cone's angle. An aircraft makes two booms, one from its nose and one from its tail.

concepts.name: Bow wakes
concepts.statement: Sonic booms are one example of a bow wake, the V-shaped disturbance created when a wave source moves faster than the wave propagation speed. Water waves spread in circles from the point where they are made, and a duck moving faster than they spread leaves the familiar wake; a subatomic particle moving through water faster than light moves in water leaves a cone of light called Cerenkov radiation.

concepts.name: Doppler shift
concepts.statement: The Doppler shift is the actual change in frequency due to relative motion of source and observer.

concepts.name: Sound interference
concepts.statement: Interference is the hallmark of waves, and one way to prove something is a wave is to observe interference effects. Sound waves in fluids are pressure waves consistent with Pascal's principle, so pressures from two sources add and subtract like simple numbers: positive and negative gauge pressures add to a much smaller pressure and a lower-intensity sound. Noise-cancelling headphones introduce a second sound with its maxima and minima exactly reversed from the incoming noise, and the beats from two similar notes played together are interference too.

concepts.name: Resonance of an air column
concepts.statement: An air column has only certain natural frequencies. A disturbance from a tuning fork travels down a tube at the speed of sound and bounces off the closed end. If the tube is just the right length, the reflected sound arrives back at the fork exactly half a cycle later and interferes constructively with the continuing sound. The incoming and reflected sounds then form a standing wave. Only the resonant frequencies interfere constructively to form standing waves, while others interfere destructively and are absent. Every sound resonance, from a bottle's toot to a singer's voice, is a matter of interference. Think of it as a natural vibration of the air column, whatever starts it.

concepts.name: Nodes and antinodes in a tube
concepts.statement: In a tube closed at one end, the standing wave has its maximum air displacement, an antinode, at the open end, where the air moves freely. It has no displacement, a node, at the closed end, where the air cannot move. The distance from a node to an antinode is one-fourth of a wavelength, so for the lowest resonance the wavelength is four times the tube's length. A tube open at both ends has antinodes at both ends and half a wavelength inside for its lowest resonance.

concepts.name: Fundamental, overtones and harmonics
concepts.statement: The lowest resonant frequency of a system is its fundamental, and all higher resonant frequencies are overtones. Every resonant frequency is an integral multiple of the fundamental, so together they are called harmonics: the fundamental is the first harmonic, the first overtone the second harmonic, and so on. For a tube closed at one end the first overtone is three times the fundamental and so is the third harmonic. Which overtones are present, and how intense they are, makes a trumpet's middle C differ from a clarinet's and one voice from another.

concepts.name: Resonances of a closed tube
concepts.statement: With one-fourth of a wavelength in the tube at the fundamental and three-fourths at the first overtone, the pattern generalises to a single expression: the resonant frequencies of a tube closed at one end are odd multiples of the speed of sound over four times the length. They depend on the speed of sound and hence on temperature, which is why musicians bring their wind instruments to room temperature before playing them together.

forms.condition: tube closed at one end, λ = 4L
tube closed at one end, λ′ = 4L/3

concepts.name: Resonances of an open tube
concepts.statement: A tube open at both ends has maximum air displacements at both ends, so its resonant frequencies are all integer multiples of the speed of sound over twice the length. Its fundamental is twice that of the same tube closed at one end, and it has a different spectrum of overtones. Two tubes with the same fundamental, one open and one closed, therefore sound different when played.

concepts.name: Finding a tube’s length or frequency
concepts.statement: To find the length of a tube that sounds a given fundamental, or the frequency a given length sounds, first find the speed of sound on the day from the air temperature. Then solve the resonance relation for the tube's kind of ends for the unknown. The same reckoning gives the range of fundamentals of the ear canal and the fraction by which an instrument's frequencies change between a cold and a warm room.

concepts.name: Resonance in musical instruments
concepts.statement: Wind instruments use resonance in air columns to amplify tones made by lips or reeds, and string instruments use sounding boxes: the vibrating string creates a sound that resonates in the box, greatly amplifying it and creating overtones that give the instrument its characteristic flavour, the more complex the box's shape the wider the range of frequencies it can resonate over. A marimba's gourds and a violin's body do the same work, and so does the cavity of the throat and mouth in speech. The ideas apply to any system with wave characteristics, down to the standing waves of an atom's electrons.

concepts.name: Antinode
concepts.statement: An antinode is a point of maximum displacement in a standing wave. In a tube it lies at an open end, where the air moves freely.

concepts.name: Node
concepts.statement: A node is a point of zero displacement in a standing wave. In a tube it lies at a closed end, where the air cannot move.

concepts.name: Fundamental
concepts.statement: The fundamental is the lowest-frequency resonance of a system.

concepts.name: Overtones
concepts.statement: Overtones are all the resonant frequencies of a system higher than the fundamental.

concepts.name: Harmonics
concepts.statement: Harmonics is the term used to refer collectively to the fundamental and its overtones, each an integral multiple of the fundamental. The fundamental is the first harmonic.

concepts.name: Audible range
concepts.statement: Normal human hearing encompasses frequencies from 20 to 20,000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound and those above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound; neither is perceived by the ear, though infrasound can sometimes be felt as vibrations. Other animals hear differently: dogs to 30,000 Hz, bats and dolphins to 100,000 Hz, elephants below 20 Hz.

concepts.name: How finely pitch is discriminated
concepts.statement: Most of us have excellent relative pitch and can tell whether one sound has a different frequency from another when the frequencies differ by 0.3% or more, so that 500.0 and 501.5 Hz are noticeably different. Pitch perception is directly related to frequency and is not greatly affected by intensity. Musical notes are particular sounds with particular names, and the uncommon ability to name one on hearing it is perfect pitch.

concepts.name: Loudness
concepts.statement: The perception of intensity is loudness. At a given frequency you can discern a difference of about 1 dB and easily notice a change of 3 dB. Loudness does not depend on intensity alone. The ear is most sensitive between 2000 and 5000 Hz, so sounds there seem louder than sounds of the same intensity at 500 or 10,000 Hz, and sounds near the extremes of the hearing range seem less loud still. The ear responds over a range of a trillion in intensity, which very few instruments can match.

concepts.name: Timbre
concepts.statement: When a violin and a piano play the same middle C there is no mistaking one for the other, because each produces a distinctive set of frequencies and intensities. Our perception of these combinations is tone quality, or timbre, described by words such as dull, brilliant, warm or rich; it is more subjective than loudness or pitch and takes the subject into perceptual psychology. A note is the basic unit of music with a specific name, and combinations of notes constitute music.

concepts.name: Reading equal-loudness curves
concepts.statement: A phon is the unit of loudness perception, as the decibel is the unit of physical intensity level, and the two are numerically equal at 1000 Hz. The equal-loudness curves relate loudness to intensity level and frequency for persons with normal hearing. Every sound along a given curve sounds equally loud. To find a sound's loudness, locate its frequency and intensity level on the grid and interpolate between the curves. To find the level a sound needs for a given loudness, follow that curve to the frequency. The curves dip between 2000 and 5000 Hz, where the ear is most sensitive, and rise at both extremes. Sounds below the 0-phon curve are not heard, and a few sounds below 0 dB are.

concepts.name: Hearing loss and audiograms
concepts.statement: Most conversational sound falls in a band of frequencies and intensity levels. With a hearing loss of 40 phons at all frequencies, you can still understand conversation, though quietly. A 60-phon loss leaves only the lowest frequencies, and you cannot understand speech unless it is much louder than normal. Hearing tests run from 250 to 8000 Hz and appear as an audiogram, whose threshold is relative to the normal threshold, so normal hearing registers as 0 dB at every frequency. Loss caused by noise shows a dip near 4000 Hz, whatever frequency caused it. The most common loss, presbycusis, comes with age and is increasingly severe at higher frequencies.

concepts.name: Hearing mechanism
concepts.statement: The ear is a transducer that converts sound waves into electrical nerve impulses. The outer ear, or ear canal, carries sound to the eardrum and resonates as an air column, which is partly why the ear is most sensitive between 2000 and 5000 Hz. The middle ear's lever system takes the force the sound pressure exerts on the eardrum, amplifies it and applies it through the oval window to the much smaller area of the cochlea. The pressure waves there are about 40 times greater than those on the eardrum. Two muscles react to intense sound in a few milliseconds and reduce the force transmitted. In the inner ear the pressure waves make the tectorial membrane vibrate against the hair cells. These resonate at different positions for different frequencies, high near the base and low at the far end. Below about 1000 Hz the nerves signal at the sound's own frequency, and above it by position. Sound can reach the cochlea through the skull when conduction fails, and a cochlear implant can stand in for lost cilia by stimulating the nerves directly.

concepts.name: Phon
concepts.statement: The phon is the numerical unit of loudness. A sound's loudness in phons is the intensity level in decibels of a 1000 Hz tone that sounds equally loud, so at 1000 Hz phons and decibels are numerically equal.

concepts.name: Note
concepts.statement: A note is a basic unit of music with a specific name, such as middle C, and notes are combined to make tunes.

concepts.name: Ultrasound
concepts.statement: Ultrasound is sound with frequencies above 20,000 Hz, the top of the range of normal human hearing. The ear does not perceive it.

concepts.name: Infrasound
concepts.statement: Infrasound is sound with frequencies below 20 Hz, the bottom of the range of normal human hearing. The ear does not perceive it, though it can sometimes be felt as vibrations.

concepts.name: Ultrasound as probe and treatment
concepts.statement: Ultrasound is any sound above 20 kHz, and its characteristics, frequency, intensity and a wavelength that limits the detail it can detect, are wave properties common to all waves. Like any wave it carries energy that the medium absorbs, with effects that vary with intensity: focused to 10³ to 10⁵ W/m² it shatters gallstones and pulverises tissue, partly through cavitation, the creation and collapse of vapour cavities; at 10³ to 10⁴ W/m² it is the deep heating of ultrasound diathermy; diagnostic intensities of about 10⁻² W/m² are too low to do thermal damage, and decades of use show no ill effects.

concepts.name: Acoustic impedance
concepts.statement: Reflections at boundaries between two media occur because of differences in their acoustic impedance, the product of a medium's density and the speed of sound through it, in kg/(m²·s). The acoustic impedances of soft tissues do not vary much, but there is a big difference between soft tissue and air and between soft tissue and bone, which is why those boundaries reflect so strongly.

concepts.name: Intensity reflection coefficient
concepts.statement: At a boundary between media of different acoustic impedance, part of the wave energy reflects and part passes through, and the greater the difference in impedance, the greater the reflection. The intensity reflection coefficient is the ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity. It is zero, total transmission, when the two impedances are the same, and an impedance match couples sound efficiently from one medium into another. An ultrasound image tracks these reflections and maps their intensity in a plane.

concepts.name: Resolution and penetration of ultrasound
concepts.statement: A transducer, a piezoelectric crystal, both sends the ultrasound and records its echoes, and the time between the signal and each echo gives the depth of each boundary at the speed of sound in tissue, about 1540 m/s. It is very difficult to detect details smaller than the wavelength of a probe: at 7 MHz the wavelength in tissue is 0.22 mm, and in practice 1 mm detail is attainable. Higher frequencies give finer detail but penetrate less, the rule of thumb being a useful depth of about 500 wavelengths, so they suit small organs such as the eye and not the deep abdomen.

concepts.name: Doppler-shifted ultrasound
concepts.statement: Ultrasound reflected from moving blood or a beating fetal heart is Doppler shifted twice. The reflector receives a shifted frequency as a moving observer and then returns it as a moving source, and the magnitude of the shift is directly proportional to the reflector's velocity. The echo adds to the broadcast frequency to produce beats, whose frequency is the absolute difference of the two. The shift itself, a few hundred hertz out of a couple of megahertz, is hard to measure. The beat frequency is easy to measure, ignores any drift in the broadcast frequency and falls in the audible range. Doppler radar measures wind, aircraft and car speeds by the same principle.
